source.title: Scaling Interpretable Transformers with Parity Bottleneck Layers
source.authors: Andrew Mack; K. Tou; Mark C. Henry; Zheng-Xun Wu; Lauren Greenspan

record.tranche_reason: The study reports SAEBench feature-absorption scores for a parity bottleneck and post-hoc SAE methods, but does not test feature splitting by increasing dictionary size.
record.gate_note: The only directly relevant reported results are the SAEBench Absorption scores in Table 4. The paper does not measure parent-child firing, whether child features partition a parent’s inputs, or feature-direction proximity. Its retrieval and causal-editing results do not test the claim versions. Statements about results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The SAEBench absorption metric derives from the absorption measure in an original source. It is reported for TopK and Matryoshka SAEs on a 1.3B dense GPT at layer 12, a new setting, but only incidentally: there is no size or sparsity sweep, no splitting analysis, and absorption is not the paper's question.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors report that the parity bottleneck shows almost zero absorption and beats TopK and Matryoshka SAEs on sparse probing and absorption, while trailing both on AutoInterp. They also note that SCR and TPP are not recommended for models under 2B parameters. They frame this as support for features native to the model's computation; they do not discuss feature splitting.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares an in-model parity bottleneck with post-hoc SAE methods using a benchmark absorption metric; it does not train increasing SAE dictionary sizes on the same activations or measure feature splits.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported absorption score differs between TopK and Matryoshka SAE methods at layer 12; the paper does not attribute this difference to size or sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: An in-model Parity Bottleneck (fixed algebraic dictionary with a fixed hierarchy, trained jointly with the LM) scores near-zero SAEBench absorption (0.01) versus 0.807 and 0.180 for post-hoc SAEs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse bottlenecks built into the model with a fixed hierarchical dictionary show little feature absorption, unlike post-hoc SAEs.

record.problems: The absorption result is a benchmark score, with no stated uncertainty or baseline in Table 4. The study does not define the score’s relation to the specific parent-child firing and input-partition behavior in V4, or test SAE size and sparsity changes.
record.rows_left_out: No other rows bear directly on the versions. The remaining results concern model capability, steering, causal editing, retrieval, or cited work rather than SAE splitting or the specified absorption behavior.

untested.parts: No dictionary-size sweep, no coarse-to-fine replacement, input coverage, or direction proximity.
No splitting analysis in large models or open SAE releases.
No nested families, geometric closeness, or concept-hierarchy mapping of SAE latents.
No test of whether changing SAE size or sparsity fixes absorption; only one SAE per architecture at one layer; no inspection of parent/child firing beyond the aggregate score.
No cross-size decomposition or novel-latent analysis.
No test of splitting as an objective artifact. The Matryoshka vs TopK absorption difference concerns absorption, not splitting, and is not analysed by the authors.

missing.what: Dictionary width and sparsity (k) of the TopK and Matryoshka SAEs used for SAEBench are not stated, so the absorption scores cannot be placed on a size or sparsity axis.

record.verdict_notes: The record lists uncertainty_reported 'y', but Table 4 gives no uncertainty; only the retrieval experiments report standard deviations. The absorption evidence is a single benchmark number per method at one layer, so the verdicts are weak. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No SAE dictionary-size sweep or measurement of coarse-feature replacement, input coverage, or direction proximity.
No test of splitting across large models or open SAE releases.
No measurement of nested feature families, geometric closeness, or correspondence to a concept hierarchy.
The study reports a benchmark feature-absorption score, but does not inspect whether a parent latent fails to fire where a child fires, nor test whether SAE size or sparsity changes that behavior.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents or measurement of novel latents.
No test attributing splitting to the SAE sparsity objective or comparing objectives as a test of splitting.

relation.reason: Its own absorption numbers for standard and Matryoshka SAEs bear on V4, though the paper's focus is its parity bottleneck.

tranche.reason: The study reports SAEBench absorption for TopK and Matryoshka SAEs on a new 1.31B dense GPT trained on FineWeb-Edu. This is a new setting with a result on absorption, though incidental to the paper's own method. It runs no size or sparsity sweep.

source_check.notes: Per Appendix G, §3.4 compares PT-Large-2L-Aux with SAEs on GPT-Large-cold (1.31B, 24 layers); layer 12 is the middle layer. The absorption values are single runs with no uncertainty, and the SAEBench SAEs' width and k are not stated. The Matryoshka contrast may also bear on V6, which has no verdict here. The paper never discusses feature splitting.
